newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Good net seen for HK & Shanghai Hotels.
newsitem.headline: Good net seen for HK & Shanghai Hotels.

text.p: Luxury hotel and property concern Hongkong and Shanghai Hotels Ltd is forecast to unveil strong earnings growth and a significant upward revision in its net asset value (NAV) for 1996 on Wednesday, analysts said.

"The price of luxury residential property almost doubled in 1996...Hongkong and Shanghai Hotels' NAV could be revised up to as high as HK$22 (US$2.84) per share," said Raymond Ngai, senior investment property analyst at UBS Securities.
As of end-1995, the company's NAV was HK$15.22 per share.
The company owns Hong Kong's prestigious Peninsula Hotel and luxury residential property, the bulk of which is in the territory's Repulse Bay district.
The consensus market forecast for the company is 27 percent earnings growth, derived chiefly from its Hong Kong operations despite a drive in recent years to expand its assets overseas.
Ngai said he was forecasting earnings of HK$804 million from core operations for the year ended December 31, 1996.

Together with HK$55 million in a one-off gain from the sale of the group's 25 percent stake in Cathay Pacific Catering Services H.K. Ltd, that will give total earnings of HK$859 million, an increase of nearly 32 percent over 1995.

In 1995, the company reported an attributable profit of HK$652 million, 98.4 percent of which was derived from Hong Kong. Some 52.5 percent was derived from hotel operations and 42.6 percent from investment properties.

In the first six months of 1996, the company reported an attributable profit of HK$435 million, including the exceptional item from the catering group sale, compared with HK$277 million in the year earlier period.
The good results were due to higher occupancy rates, leading to higher room rates and greater profitability, and to an end to losses in the company's Peninsula New York.

"Average occupancy rates at Hong Kong's hotels in 1996 were higher than in previous years, but the rates were boosted by a decline in room supply," Mark Tsang of Nikko Research Center (HK) said in a recent report.

Ngai said he believed the Peninsula Hong Kong recorded an occupancy rate of 73 percent in 1996 compared with 72 percent in 1995, and that room rates rose an average six percent to HK$3,350 during the year.
Tsang estimated an average room rate of HK$3,470 per night.
In all, the company should have been able to raise its operating profit margin to 40 percent in 1996 from 35 percent in 1995.

Another reason for the jump in profitability will be an improvement in the contribution from the Peninsula New York, which should break even -- for the first time -- in 1996 and show an operating profit of HK$11 million in 1997, said Tsang.
The company said that in the first six months of 1996, the New York hotel achieved an average room rate of US$332 and an occupancy of 75 percent.
The one wild card in the group's earnings outlook is the treatment of heavy capitalised interest charges on loans taken out for the development of the much delayed Peninsula Bangkok, said Ngai.

"My forecast includes a HK$100 million provision for these interest rate charges," said Ngai, adding it would not be prudent to capitalise all the interest charges related to the two-year delay in the construction of the hotel.
Management have said they were planning a soft opening for this hotel in mid-1997.

Another factor clouding the outlook is the group's HK$1.18 billion development in Australia near the Sydney Opera House. Critics and demonstrators have demanded an end to the project, saying it blocks the view of the Sydney Opera House, one of Australia's prime tourist attractions.
